utterances.text: In connection with the question of the arming of the Mujahedin and logistics, I wish to show you a few more documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before that, Your Honour, may this document be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 336.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the witness now have a look at D345. These are again excerpts from his book.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, will you look through at page 06050726. Do you agree that in a part of your book you describe the work of Islamic humanitarian organisations in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at this page now, please. It is entitled "Kuwaiti Humanitarian Organisation." Can you see that? And will you please read through the text under this heading. And in this connection I have the following question for you: Do you agree that you said that while you were a commander of the Mujahedin unit in Bijelo Bucje you received funds for the needs of the unit from a Kuwaiti humanitarian organisation? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, will you please look at the page 06050731. Can you look at that page, please? To save time, please focus on eight or nine lines from the top when you say: "When I was a commander of a unit in Bijelo Bucje." This is page 3 of the English version, beginning: "When I was commander of the unit in Bijelo Bucje near Travnik." I believe, Witness, that by now you have read this excerpt, and I would like to ask you the following: You described here that while you were the commander you also received humanitarian aid from several other Islamic organisations. And not only from the Kuwaiti, among them the Third World Organisation.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Please look now at page 06050737. And I draw your attention, Witness, to the bottom part of this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is page 4 in the English version, beginning about 10 or 12 lines from the top, "Under very strange circumstances, general director Naser."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, for you I have a question. Do you agree that you're describing here the activities it of the Balkan Islamic centre in Zenica? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in this excerpt you say that you were given considerable assistance with money and food for members of the El Mujahedin Detachment and El Zuhayr's unit.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there's a mistake here. We're talking about the High Saudi Committee.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then I'm wrong. Is it true that what I'm asking you, that is that the Saudi committee assisted the El Mujahedin Detachment as well as members of Zubeir's unit? But your conclusion was that Zubeir's unit received more assistance. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wish to ask you the following: In addition to the El Mujahedin unit, the Mujahedin administration also formed a unit called Abu Zubeir?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that the Mujahedin Detachment formed it, but the main al-Qaeda cell outside Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I understand. So the main allocate a cell outside Bosnia and Herzegovina formed the El Mujahedin Detachment. And who formed the Abu Zubeir unit?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also an al-Qaeda cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can this document be admitted into evidence and given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 337.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the witness now look at document D346 regarding this same topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I wish to draw your attention to this first paragraph when you see the name Talal Filal. This is also at the top of the page in the English version. Witness, will you just read that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Did you know Talal Filal, son of Hasan?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me quote from this document. "When the three of them set up the Islamic Centre Balkan in Zenica, the aim of which was to spread the faith --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have read the first paragraph. Now, where are you reading now?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. The eighth line of the English version. It begins with the words "The three of them."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it says here that: "The Balkan Islamic Centre in Zenica, whose aim was to spread Islam and provide welfare and humanitarian help to the needy. These two organisations and some other humanitarian organisations from Arab countries (Elaharamine) [phoen], were used as logistic support for the El Mujahedin Detachment." I want to ask you whether you knew anything about the Balkan Islamic Centre.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know a little about it, and I described this in my book.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this document contains correct information regarding assistance given to the detachment? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, because I have a different opinion of that centre and the people who headed that centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell us what your opinion is?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that foreign Mujahedin headed that centre. In public they claimed it was intended to spread Islam, but in fact it was al-Qaeda activities in Bosnia during the war. They attempted in this way to -- to spread the belief among domestic Mujahedin similarly to the beliefs that foreign Mujahedins had.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In what way would they win them over, by giving them material assistance?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, quite a number of young people came to study real Islam, and they taught them incorrectly, telling them that real Islam is violence over all those who do not belong to that faith, but they also gave them financial aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this Islamic centre assisted financially whom?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: People who came regularly to that centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the premises of the Balkan Islamic Centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can this document be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 338.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In connection with this same issue, Your Honour, could the witness look at document D347. It is an excerpt from an official record on intercepted conversations, dated the 23rd of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you, Witness, please, look at page 4 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is page 5 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And, Witness, will you look at paragraphs from 16 to 20. Page 5 of the English version, paragraphs from 16 through 20. Will you please look at the names that are mentioned here. Do you agree with me that this refers to a conversation between Abu Talib and Abu Ma'ali? You're familiar with the name Abu Ma'ali. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was they were the head of a Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Abu Talib perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it says here that Alib [phoen] asked for money to purchase weapons?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you this. Please look further down. Do you know Abu Hajir?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Abu Rachid?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Abu Eymen?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you see here conversations among these people with Arabic names regarding the procurement of weapons. Did you know that the Mujahedin did obtain weapons for themselves with their own money?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that they purchased weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can this document be given an exhibit number, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 339.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, during your testimony yesterday, you said on a number of occasions that the Mujahedin were under the command of the army, that is, within the composition of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What I would like to put to you is the following: The Mujahedin in Bosnia and Herzegovina actually were never under the command of the army. Local commanders never gave orders to them. I'm talking about commands and not cooperation. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree. First of all, we foreign Mujahedin did not participate in any battle without cooperating with the BH army -- or, rather, the local commanders decided the locations where we would attack. Then they would ask us for our assistance, and then we would take part in that operation but on condition that we, too, have to carry out surveillance of the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And during those operations you received orders from your commanders?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because whichever battle we agreed to take part in, we set as a precondition to the Bosnian commanders that during the attack itself we should be in command, and they agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So the -- your precondition for participating in the operation was that you should be in command. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Testifying yesterday, Witness, you mentioned the name Abdul, and I apologise if I mispronounce it, Abuladim Maqtouf as one of the interpreters for the Mujahedin. Do you remember mentioning that?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was not a member of the El Mujahedin unit?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not a member.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the person who was convicted by an effective judgement for participation in hijack -- in the kidnapping?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what is your position about this? Was this person guilty? I don't want you to recount this event. I just want to hear what you view is. Was the person guilt or not?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that person was not guilty for the crime for which he was convicted.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I now wish to ask you, do you remember that you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of the State Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina against the accused Abduladim Maqtouf to Jonathan Smith on the 9th of May, 2005? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you now please look at that statement. It is D348. First of all, take a look at the second page of the document. Take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you have it in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, since the document was compiled before a Bosnian court, the Bosnian version is signed. Witness, do you agree that you signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So can you please take a look at the second page. No. Actually, it's page number 5 in Bosnian, and in English it's page number 4. So number 4 in English, and for you number 5. Have you found it, page number 5? I'm now going to quote a short excerpt from -- from your conversation with the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor asks: "You say al-Qaeda. There was no al-Qaeda organisation in BiH."

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnian it's number 4, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My mistake.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So the Prosecutor: "You say al-Qaeda. There was no al-Qaeda organisation in BiH." You say: "It is not true." Prosecutor: "There were soldiers who fought, but there was no al-Qaeda organisation." You answer: "That is not true, because al-Qaeda organised the arrival of Mujahedins to be BiH. Their people were the leaders of those forces." Prosecutor: "Including El Mujahid unit?" And you answer: "Yes." Therefore, you said here that people from al-Qaeda headed the detachment and commanded the detachment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also clearly stated that al-Qaeda organised the arrival of those people to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, isn't it improbable that the commanders of a poor army of Bosnia and Herzegovina would command the chiefs of al-Qaeda, what you are attempting to say here?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, briefly I can only state that we, the foreign Mujahedins, from the very arrival to Bosnia during the war, that we haven't actually arrived here to help the Bosnian people. It is true that we have stated that, but we had our secret goals unknown to local people. Not those from the BiH army, and also not the leadership, Izetbegovic and others who led the country during the war. In my book, I wrote a text headed "The Connections Between The Current Leadership of the BiH and the Mujahedins." So I state that there was a connection between the BiH army and Mujahedins, and what I say is that they were controlled by the BiH army, I mean the Mujahedins, but they didn't know and what those foreign Mujahedins were precisely because we tried to hide those things from them. I mean, al-Qaeda activities. We arrived here on a mission there al-Qaeda.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute here. I have just given you a part of your statement given to the international state prosecutor here. I think it was Jonathan Smith. There you say that members of al-Qaeda commanded Mujahedins. How could the BH army then control them? How can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was different kinds of commands. For instance, if you talk about El Misri, one of the chiefs of the Mujahedin, he had contact with the people who had come from outside the BiH. He would be the one who would report about a situation. So for instance, if al-Qaeda would refuse that we take part in an attack, then we wouldn't take part in that attack even with the BiH army would request -- would request us. So if al-Qaeda would give permission to take part in an attack, it would mean that we would have to cooperate with the BiH army. It means that al-Qaeda was on top of everything for us, the foreign Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, I'm satisfied with this answer. Now, can you take a look at D349.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And of course I should like to ask the previous document be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The previous document 348 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 340.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, D349, page number 06050631. So what I'm interested in is line number six where it says: "This unit was merged with the Mujahedin unit called Zubeir 's unit." I want to ask you a question in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, Your Honours, you have the passage here, and it says: "This unit was merged with the Mujahedin unit called Zubeir's unit."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, here you state: "This unit was merged with the Mujahedin unit called Zubeir's unit. I, however, was not under the command of the Green Berets but Zubeir's unit. Otherwise, the Mujahedin position was always the same. Mujahedin should be commanded by the Mujahedin and the Bosniaks by the Bosniaks. We will cooperate and work together with them, but we shall not accept any orders from them. We can only accept proposals which then we may accept or not. This was al-Qaeda position of which I was aware even before I came to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it had never been violated."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam Vidovic. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps before, if the witness answers, if we could be given a time period in which this part of the witness's book relates. I think we've been shown a huge number of excerpts from his book. This excerpt in particular, I believe, needs to have a particular date reference for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, and so I would ask my learned colleague if she could provide us or perhaps ask the witness to provide us with the time period in which this excerpt of his book relates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, here you describe activities of Zubeir's unit, and all of us here really want to know whether you remember what time period is it, your description here. Did I understand it correctly that it was 1995?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the period from 1994 until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, does this satisfy you? Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So let's finish this thing here. It says here: "Work together with them but not accept any orders from them, only proposals, which then we may accept or not. This was al-Qaeda position of which I have been aware before I came to BiH, and it had never been violated in this area during the entire war." Now, Witness, it is correct, isn't it, that you described here actual relations between the Bosniaks and the Mujahedins? The al-Qaeda rules was in force when it comes to the Mujahedins?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now just a brief question related to Abu Zubeir's unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is having very important for us right now, but before that I should ask that this document be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 341.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You remember that when you gave the statement to the Prosecutor in August 2006 you gave a detailed description of the Abu Zubeir's unit.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, first of all, you knew Mr. Abu Zubeir very well?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us his physical description? Was there something characteristic about him?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he looked a bit fat, a bit slow. He didn't look like a military-able man.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, he was big. He was fat. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like the witness to take a look at D350. For the record, that's an excerpt from the book written by Evan Kohlmann titled "Al-Qaeda's Jihad in Europe." In Bosnian it's page 52. In English it's the second page in English here. It begins with words "Like Abu Sulajman [phoen], Abu Zubeir al Haili."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that Witness, the beginning of this page? It says here: "Like Abu Sulajman, Abu Zubeir al Haili, also known as 'The Bear,' a 300 pound monster of a man, had also first gained the reputation as a fearless and calculating military commander in Afghanistan before serving as an artillery expert with the Arab Mujahedin in Bosnia. Until recently, Abu Zubeir was a resident of Tooting, South London, where he regularly sent young recruits from the West to Taliban and al-Qaeda training camps in central Asia. He came from the same area of Saudi Arabia as bin Laden and had first fought alongside the infamous al-Qaeda chief during the Soviet-Afghan war. Two years ago, The Bear even reportedly helped coordinate the escape of Osama bin Laden from the collapsing Tora Bora cave complex." Now, I'm interested in description of this person. The person described in here, is that the person that you call Abu Zubeir?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used to call him Abu Zubeir al Haili, that's true, but this other name is unknown to me, so I'm not quite sure whether it's the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you about the physical description.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, physically, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The name is unknown, The Bear?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: "Abu Zubeir al Haili," did you say that?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said you know that name, but you also said, "This other name I do not know," and I'm -- my question is which other name is this that you don't know? Is that the name that calls him The Bear or anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Excuse me. You didn't understand me. Here they say that this person has, among other names, also Abu Zubeir al Haili. In answer to the question of Defence whether it was the same person that I was referring to, I said maybe. Maybe it is, maybe it isn't. Because this name here, Abu Zubeir al Haili, is the name that I know, but his characteristics contained in here are not known to me. That is why I cannot conclude whether that's the same person or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honours, for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, the description in book, is that the physical description of Abu Zubeir that you know? He's a big man?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can we assign an exhibit to this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 342.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now, Witness, I would like to remind you again of the statement you gave to the investigators of the -- of the Prosecutor on the 15th of August, 2006, if I'm not mistaken. Do you remember that you drew a very detailed diagram of the attack, and it was attachment B to your statement of the 15th of August? First of all, can you take a look at D352? You will then understand what I'm referring to. D352.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me explain. I did request a translation of the entirety of the text contained in this document. However, you know the problems. I really don't have to explain these things. You know that the Translation Unit has lots of work, so we only have here a small translation of the part of the text in the left upper corner and the left lower corner. When I receive the whole translation of the document, I'm going to attach it. In other words, I'm going to replace this incomplete translation with the complete translation. However, right now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps -- my learned colleague has made reference to an attack. Perhaps if she can again for the record indicate the date that this diagram relates to, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. First I wanted the witness to take a look at the map, and then I would of course go on and ask the very question that my colleague, Prosecutor, now mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement given to the Prosecutor you described events relate -- related to the attack on Vozuca in September 1995. Am I correct? I'm talking here about your statement to the Prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So that's the attack. Now, can you take a look at your drawing, and can you confirm that you have indeed drawn this in your own hand, signed, and then handed over to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 17th of August, 2006?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the same drawing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like this document to be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, here you have described the movements of certain units such as El Mujahedin and Abu Zubeir during the attack; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 343.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, now I would like to pose a brief question related to a person that you maybe know. I'm going to ask you do you know Ahmed Zuhayr aka Handala?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like the witness to take a look at D354.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And before we start working with this document, it is correct, isn't it, that in September 1995, in combat activities, this person also took part along with his group? I am talking about Ahmed Zuhayr Handala.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. He took part in this action, but he was an ordinary soldier under my command.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. But you haven't really understood my question. I haven't really said if he was in the Abu Zubeir's unit. I simply said he did take part in combat activities in 1995.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, take a look at D354.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, this is a statement given to the FBI investigators related to the murder of William Arnold Jefferson on 18th of November, 1995. Your Honour, we have that statement in English. We are interested in the second paragraph. Second paragraph on the first page of the statement, both in Bosnian and English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you stated that: "Handala left the Mujahedins due to a misunderstanding. He wanted to form his own unit, and he had good connections with Osama bin Laden, and Osama bin Laden respected what Handala wanted to do with his group. Handala, aka Zuhayr, convinced member of the Mujahedin's Light Brigade and other young members to join his unit. It was Handala's plan to develop the young members of his unit to become the future members of the unit." So I understand that Handala, in 1995, was not a member of El Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like this document to be assigned an exhibit number. Your Honour, maybe this is also a convenient moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 344.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic, I did know that you did ask at the beginning of your cross-examination that you be given slightly more time than the Prosecution did get. You will -- you are left with about 10 minutes to the end of your first three hours. Just think about that during the break. We will take a break and a come back at 1.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, before the break we talked about Zuhayr, and now I would like you to look at document D355. D355?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, I would like to say that this is an article published in the Oslobodjenje daily on the 7th of December, 1997, and the title of the article is "Zuhayr is the Real Handala."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I can see that you put your glasses on. Can you please look at this photograph and the ID document, and I'm asking you the following: The person from this ID card, is that Handala Zuhayr, the same Handala that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, now I'm going to read to you the beginning of the text, this article from the Oslobodjenje daily of the 7th of December, 1997. It is says -- it says: "Ahmed Zuhayr, whose official identity card issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Croatia was published in yesterday's Oslobodjenje, is the real Handala suspected of being a high-ranking terrorist in these areas." And then at the bottom of the article...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: ... there is another excerpt just underneath the photograph, and it says: "Zuhayr is a Saudi but most probably worked for several intelligence services." I would like to ask you this: Is Zuhayr from -- is he a Saudi by origin?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he's a Yemeni, but he had a Saudi passport.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell me if you had information that he worked for intelligence services?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have that information. I learned that only during questioning. But before that I noticed that he had some secret contacts with the HVO military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He had contacts with the military police of the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When did you notice that?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him or had meetings with him from 1994 until the end of the war. Before being arrested in 1995, he moved around in territories that were under the control of the HVO without difficulties while other Mujahedin were not able to do so. Sometimes he was escorted by HVO police vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now I would like the witness to look -- oh, and also can this document be given an exhibit number, please, this article?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 345.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would now like you to look at D356. This is an interview that you gave on the 26th of June, 2007, to the Glas Javnosti magazine. Witness I would like to ask you to first tell us if you did provide this interview. Can you look, please? And it's dated the 26th of June, 2007.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at page 2 of this interview. I am going to ask you the following: Can you please look at this part when you are being asked: "Why was that building demolished? What was that for?" Could you see that part?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The journalist asked you about the crime that you were sentenced for as an accomplice, and you talked about the person who was convicted together with you for the same crime. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read a part out to you. You said that he worked for al-Qaeda and also the Croatian Secret Service. Which jobs did he do for al-Qaeda and which ones did he do for al-Qaeda [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know if Croatia knew he was an al-Qaeda man, but I know that on one occasion he was allowed to come from Croatia with a truck full of weapons which were handed over to the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Were you talking here about Ahmed Zuhayr Handala or someone else?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: About Ahmed Zuhayr.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you had information that he worked for the Croatian Secret Service?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeated what I was told during questioning by the Bosnia and Herzegovina MUP, but before that I suspected that he was cooperating with the Secret Service, which was then confirmed to me by the inspector during my questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Forget the inspectors now. Can you tell me -- and I'm talking about your personal knowledge now, not what you heard from others. What did you personally know about this cooperation? Did you know about this truck with weapons?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about this truck with weapons, I wasn't present, but he confirmed that himself. And I know that the Mujahedin in Travnik -- or, rather, in Zenica received plenty of weapons through him. So this confirmed to me that he was speaking the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what was he saying?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he came from Croatia with a full truck of weapons and that he managed to enter Bosnia without any problems, and then he handed these weapons over to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this document be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 346.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would now like to clarify one more thing with you. You described at one point -- or you said that Abdel Aziz told you about his contacts with Izetbegovic, and then you said some other Bosniak Muslims had contacts with al-Qaeda representatives. Did I understand you correctly, that you said that at the time you did not know anything about the al-Qaeda organisation itself? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you thinking about Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I didn't know about that, or they didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that al-Qaeda and its actions became a topic only after 11th of September?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So the local Muslims considered them Arabs. They didn't have any idea about al-Qaeda at that time. Is that what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 11th of September of which, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2001. And I hope I am not mistaken in that year. If I have made a mistake, I apologise, but it's 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you said that it is your evidence that the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina didn't know anything about al-Qaeda until the 11th of September, 2001? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say that, yes, but I'm thinking of the people, not about the authorities or people in authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in that case just one more clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, when you were describing these contacts of individuals from the Bosnian leadership, did I understand you correctly that you said that they, at the time during the war, did not know that the Arabs --

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not during the wartime, only after the war. Only then was this discussed in international institutions. So local organs didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That these were al-Qaeda members actually?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamed, I just want to return to a couple of questions raised both by the Defence and in the question that the Presiding Judge just put to you. When you say the authorities may have known about al-Qaeda, who -- whom are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the police, the intelligence people. I said and I wrote in my book that they didn't know about that, but we cannot rule out the possibility that some of them did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in response to a number of questions put to you by Mrs. Vidovic, you elaborated upon an earlier answer you'd given me concerning a meeting between Ebu Abdel Aziz and President Izetbegovic, and my question to you, sir, is are you aware of any other instance where foreign Mujahedin or foreign Mujahedin leaders met with President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard something in conversations with Mujahedin. I was a unit commander at the beginning of the war, and all my interest was focused on my own unit, meaning that I did not pay attention to these other affairs, contacts with the political and military leadership in Sarajevo. Also, when the Mujahedin Detachment was formed, I learned through conversations with Mujahedin from the El Mujahedin Detachment that they had travelled to Sarajevo on several occasions where they had meetings with Izetbegovic and with several important people who were in the leadership of the country during the war and that they met with the military leadership, but they didn't name the persons involved specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And for purposes of clarification, Mr. Hamed, were you in at any point a member of the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the El Mujahedin Detachment, but I can say that this was before the formation of the El Mujahedin Detachment. When I left the Mujahedin groups that were billeted in Travnik and Mehurici, then a short time after that they formed they formed the El Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with a publication of President Izetbegovic called "The Islamic Declaration"?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamed, did you ever hear about a military unit called the Bosanska Krajina Operations Group?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamed, you were asked a number of times by the Defence about orders received by the foreign Mujahedin from Bosnian army generals. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you simply tell us, sir, during the period when you were the commander of the Mujahedin unit in Bijelo Bucje in the first half of 1993 how the cooperation was between your unit, the local units, and your commander, Wahiuddin, who was in Mehurici? Can you describe that relationship for the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they had a plan, and I'm thinking about the B and H army units, to attack any location which would be too hard for them, they would come to me and they would ask me to take part in the same attack. I would then voice my willingness to do that, but under the condition that this be told to me by Wahiuddin, and then they would get in touch with him and he would approve that. Then I would personally have to get in touch with Wahiuddin and hear from him personally that I was given a green light, because, frankly speaking, I didn't have too much confidence in the armija units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But say, sir, that they would get in touch with Wahiuddin, who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm thinking of several company commanders who were billeted in Travnik. I'm thinking of, for example, Vahid Dervisevic, one of the commanders of the 317th Krajina Brigade. I'm thinking of -- there were a few, in any case, but I cannot recall the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honours. The Prosecution has no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. Judge? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you spoke to us, if I'm not mistaken, about and intervention by General Alagic. In fact, an intervention by threats in order to prevent the Mujahedin destroying the church at Guca Gora, and he succeeded you told us. I would like to know, to the best of your knowledge, whether commanders of Bosnian army units intervened on other occasions to prevent criminal activities by the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hamed, I have two sets of questions for you. The first set of questions relates to the technical operations on the ground, and the reason I'm putting these questions to you is that I need to ascertain just how was the responsibility divided between the ABiH command and your command over your troops. I understand from your testimony yesterday and today that your involvement in combat operations would always begin -- or at least would frequently begin by a request made by the local ABiH commander to -- either to you or to Wahiuddin for assistance from the Mujahedin soldiers to engage in a combat operation that the ABiH wanted to carry out. So the initiative was always -- or at least most frequently taken by the ABiH. And then your involvement would then depend on acceptance from Wahiuddin, meaning that you would not engage in any combat operations unless you had the green light from him. Have I understood this correctly?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Then how was the operation normally planned? Now closely were the details arranged between you and the ABiH forces on the technical level? Can you clarify this a bit?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the first steps we needed to reconnoiter the terrain where the attack was supposed to be carried out. So we as foreigners were not as familiar with the terrain as the local people were. So I would pick a few men from my units who were able to communicate with the local people, and then the other unit that comprised Bosniaks would also choose a few men, and then they would together carry out the reconnaissance of the terrain, and it would take maybe two or three days, maybe more, maybe less. And then after that, if we needed some equipment or weapons that we were lacking we would take it from them. We were also provided with food. Then we would agree when the attack would begin. So there had to be an agreement. They would not order us when to attack, but they would suggest a time for us, and we would accept that proposal. In case their proposal did not suit us, then we would not participate in that attack. Then we would set off together to attack, but us foreign fighters would always be in the first strike. They would mostly ask us for help when they felt that they could not liberate an area or an elevation by themselves, meaning that we were going first. We would seize the location. Then we would continue with the attack, and then they would secure and guard the locations that we had liberated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you choose which route for your soldiers to follow, or was that something that was also done in agreement? What I mean was that when you begin an operation, let's say you want to take control over a mountain, then your soldiers might go either right or left or go straight up, but who took the position -- who took the decision to -- to choose the routes that your soldiers would follow? Would that be you or would that be done in agreement?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be done in agreement, or the proposal would always come from them because they were more familiar with the terrain than we were. And then after surveying or reconnoitering the terrain we would accept the proposal if it suited us too. If it did not suit us, for example, the place where the attack would begin, we would give our proposal. If they refused or rejected our proposal, then - they sometimes used to do that - then we would move to the conditions or terms. Either the attack would be done the way we wanted it done or we would not participation in the action. So in that case, they would accept our terms and the attack would be executed the way we planned and asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Then during the operation I suppose you would have to act as commander quite independently in the action itself. When the attack physically began, then, I suppose, that you as a commander would then direct your soldiers to attack this house or to seize this valley in the sense that -- that at that point during the operation to would be too difficult to enter into any negotiations and agreement about the physical exercise of the operation, the carrying out of the operation. So my question to you is: Once the operation was -- was started, would there then still be cooperation and negotiation between the ABiH and you, or would you at that time be the commander of your forces alone?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depended on whether an agreement was reached about that attack or if we had set pre-conditions that they accepted. If it was a joint endeavour, then we would only go as far as we were told to go, that we shouldn't go any further than that. However, if it is an attack in which we demanded that we play the main role, then we would capture the location that they were interested in, but we would frequently go further on and they would follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: All right. Subsequent to attacks, would you then report back to Wahiuddin or to the ABiH on the -- on the progress of the attack? I mean, after the attack had been completed, then who would you report to?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would first inform Wahiuddin, and then I would communicate by way of radio with the commanders of the units who took part in the same operation to see what next. Should we withdraw, retreat, or is there a follow-up to this plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, suppose you -- or maybe I should ask in a different way. Did you ever during any of the operations that you commanded become aware of irregularities committed by your own troops?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this did happen, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could you give one or two examples of such irregularities, and also explain to the Chamber which actions you took?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, when I was commander of a unit in Bijelo Bucje, we had contact with Bosniak units regarding military activities, so that frequently Bosniaks would come to see me who could speak Arabic. One of my soldiers, an Egyptian, Abu Handala, wanted to kill one of the leaders of Bosniak units in Bijelo Bucje. It is Zuhdija Adilovic. He tried to persuade me that we should do that, accusing him of allowing the Bosniaks to drink alcohol, and Islam prohibits this. He also accused him of secretly collaborating with the HVO, of endeavouring to destroy Islam and eliminate it from the hearts of Bosniak youth. I didn't allow it, and this didn't happen. Another example I would choose dates back to 1995. During an attack on Vozuca, at the beginning of the attack I led a group. I was on the right flank or the right side of the small town, and in front of us was Vozuca. From the middle of the attack until the end I led all the Mujahedin, because the main leader of that operation was wounded and he had to go back. And I remember that a man appeared from a trench, a Serb soldier. I assume he was about 45 years old. And as he raised his rifle, he said that he wanted to surrender, and he begged us not to kill him. I did not allow the soldiers to shoot at him, and I told him that everything would be okay, he just had to put his rifle on the ground and to approach. He did that. And my intention was to save his life, but I didn't know what to do with him because the battle was ongoing, and we were still being shot at, and we still had to hide behind trees. So I told him, "Everything will be okay. Just stay by me." He cried, and he said -- he begged me, "Please don't kill me. I have three children." I protected him as much as I could from the Mujahedin. However, my fighters attacked him physically, and I couldn't prevent it. When they saw that they couldn't kill him, then they said, "Let us at least physically hurt him." The soldier probably didn't trust me, and I don't blame him for not trusting me. Who would have trusted me in such circumstances? Not a single Serb soldier would have trust me if I were to say to him, "Don't run away. I'll spare your life." So I was busy, occupied with the shooting that we were exposed to, and there was the shooting coming from a wood, and he took advantage of my lack of attention and he fled, but he chose the wrong side. He in fact ran towards another group of Mujahedin led by Abid Ash Shargi, a Saudi who took part in the attack as the commander of a group. I don't know what happened to him, but later, upon the completion of that operation, I learnt that the Mujahedin who were under the command of Abid Ash Shargi had killed him. That is, that they had shot at him. And after that, a commander of mine, Abid, approached him and severed his head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if he was taken prisoner before he was killed?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't take him prisoner. They opened fire at him, because this Serb soldier didn't stop running.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's just move back a little bit to the violence that your people administered to him while he was still with your group. Did you ever take any action to reproach your men, to say that this is not lawful to attack a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? There was an interruption, so I didn't hear your whole question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry. My question was if you ever raised the incident again with your troops to reproach them for having hit the Serb soldier while he was under your command, under your protection.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did everything I could at that point in time. I stood between the Serb soldier and a group of my fighters who were -- wanted to assault him. I didn't dare, nor did I have the authority to take any steps against them, because I was the commander of a group during the attack, but I wasn't the overall commander of Zubeir's unit. So this should have been done by the main commander. What I did was to inform my superior, Abu Zubeir, about the whole event, what they did, what I did to prevent it, but Abu Zubeir considered me to be wrong. He felt that what I did was helping Christians, and he supported what my soldiers did. I also informed Sead Rekic [phoen] about this. Sead Rekic was a major and had a special unit within the 3rd Corps under the commands of Sakib Mahmuljin, and he simply said that there was nothing he could do. I also informed Sakib Mahmuljin personally about this event. He simply did not react to what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Your answer to me begs the question of whether your troops, and yourself, indeed, knew the laws of the war as they are laid down in the Geneva Conventions and whether you were ready to abide by these rules. Did you recognise the Geneva Conventions in your combat operations?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt a little about this, but let me tell you just one thing. During that period of time, I was a bad person. I engaged in bad activities, and I can tell you that I wasn't really interested in the things you just mentioned. But there's one thing in my mind. It is true that I was a bad person, an evil person, and that I did some evil things, but I wasn't aggressive. So my position, even while I was the unit commander, if I attack a particular location, I'm interested in that location alone. I seek to spare the lives of my fighters and the lives on the opposite side, because I was taught in the bin Laden school in Afghanistan if you attack a nation, a group of people, and you surround them from all sides, they may be much weaker than you, but they will have to fight against you with all available means because that would be a matter of life and death. And that is why I didn't like to do that. Whenever I attacked or took part in an operation against the army of Republika Srpska or the HVO, I gave them an hour and a half advance warning that we were marching. So I would shoot at the targets and then standstill with my soldiers for about an hour and a half. And once I knew that there was no one left in the village, I would enter the house with a small group, although -- enter the village and the houses to see whether there were any people left. Then I would enter [as interpreted] my other fighters to enter. But I always said that they must the kill a prisoner. If they come across a wounded person, that they mustn't kill him but that they should give him aid. And I personally helped Croatian soldiers and took them to a hospital. I even threatened my own soldiers and said, "Should such a thing happen, if I hear of a woman being raped, that I would have to kill that fighter." And that is precisely why I was removed from the position of commander but -- because this kind of approach did not suit my -- my bosses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you, during your training in -- with the al-Qaeda -- before your arrival to Bosnia, did training -- or information about the Geneva Conventions -- was that a part -- was that a part of your training, your military training by the al-Qaeda, or were the Geneva Conventions ever mentioned during the training?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mentioned during the training, but we called it differently. We call -- we rejected it. The main al-Qaeda cells rejected all these rules. We called it Taguts [phoen], because al-Qaeda had quite different rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I apologise for taking time into looking into these issues, but I think they're quite relevant. So my question would be were the rules that you were taught at al-Qaeda, were they in conformity with, shall we say, the basic principles of the Geneva Conventions, or were they completely different?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were quite the opposite, completely the opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me then move to my second line of questions, and this line of questions relate to the possibility of taking actions towards or against people who had committed offences during the combat operations. You told us about a trial that you a part in because you had been accused of something and a trial was then held against you conducted by the Mujahedin. My question was, first of all, what were you accused of at that trial?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see. What I told you about my rules during operations did not suit the Mujahedin leaders in Bosnia. I was arrested because of the first attack on a mountain called Mescama near Travnik, near the village of Bijelo Bucje where my unit was billeted. During the attack I held a speech to all my soldiers and said that there must be no rapes; that anybody trying to escape should not be killed, even people shooting at a us from a distance we shouldn't shoot back, but we would just avoid being hit; that we must assisted wounded. And I took two wounded men to hospital. This was one of the reasons why they held me before something like a military court, and Imad [phoen] El Misri asked me whether I was doing this to assist the Croats. "Have we come to Bosnia to help the Croats, to save their lives, or to kill each and every one of them?" So they demanded of me to kill everyone. And when we attacked something that not a single person should be left alive, even animals. But I didn't do that. The second reason why I was tried -- this was in secret and all the members of the Mujahedin unit didn't know about it but only a group of people linked to al-Qaeda. My refusal to obey Wahiuddin's orders meant for them that I was rejecting the orders of al-Qaeda, and they considered this as an indication that I wanted to abandon them. Let me add there was a small misunderstanding between me and the leaders of the Mujahedin forces, so I was replaced from my duties. I was insulted, I felt offended, and I left them for a while and joined the 317th Krajina Brigade. From -- in that short period I contacted only local people and had no contact at all with the Mujahedin. They felt that my intention was to withdraw not only from the Mujahedin forces there but from al-Qaeda which had sent me here, and that is why the decision was taken to arrest me. I must also add that I am still claiming that local people, and I am referring to the Bosniaks, didn't know who and what we were. They didn't know that our coming to Bosnia was part of al-Qaeda's programme in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They didn't know that we were linked to al-Qaeda. They simply knew that we had come here to help the Muslims. I wish to tell everyone that the Bosniaks, no ordinary foreign Mujahedin, knew that I was linked to al-Qaeda. They didn't know that the leaders of the Mujahedin forces were linked to al-Qaeda. We sought to conceal our links to al-Qaeda. And the trial went as follows: That I would be secretly questioned. I would be alone and only then we would talk about al-Qaeda and why I was rejecting orders and withdrawing from al-Qaeda. They tried to persuade me that I should rejoin the Mujahedin in order for my life to be spared. There was also a public trial held -- I think it was in Mehuric -- no, in Orasje where the Mujahedin camp was, and there were quite a number of Bosniaks who watched this trial. At that trial some other reasons were given for my arrest so that these Bosniaks would not discover the al-Qaeda activities in Bosnia. Like, for instance, that I had smuggled cigarettes, that I had come to Bosnia just to get in touch with women, to drink alcohol, which is wrong. And then I was sentenced to 20 days of prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you at any point become aware of attempts made by the ABiH to take action against crimes committed by Mujahedin troops, for instance, looting or killing of prisoners or torture or inhumane treatment? Crimes that we have heard during this trial did occur and were probably committed at some occasions by Mujahedin troops and which were brought to the knowledge of the ABiH commanders. My question is: Was there any -- was there ever any action taken from the ABiH to discipline or perhaps prosecute members of the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge this did not happen once during the war or after the war. Allow me to tell you something. After my arrest in 1997, but this is linked to your question, I tried to get in touch with certain responsible officials here in Bosnia, and I told them a hundred times about the crimes committed by the Mujahedin. Policemen came to see me, intelligence officers, too, and I told them about several killings of Serb and Croatian civilians. I told them where these crime had been committed, where and when and who were the perpetrators of those crimes. However, to this day I don't see that anything has been done in concrete terms. But let me go back to the time of war. In 1995, an operation was carried out at Vozuca and Ozren. Participating in this operation were many Bosniak units. The organiser of that operation was the -- the generals of the 3rd and the 2nd Corps. We foreign Mujahedin did participate in the attack. Mujahedin Detachment attacked Vozuca from Paljenik. I was in Zubeir's unit at the time. I'm talking about Zubeir's unit. We attacked Vozuca from a mountain called Gradic. Gradic and Paljenik are two high mountains, and between them in the valley is Vozuca, which means that we attacked from two sides. When I came down with my soldiers to Vozuca, I remember that it was deserted. There was no one there. I saw quite a number of foreign fighters, Mujahedin Detachments. I also saw a large number of Bosniak units. I was there with Sead Brkic. He didn't participate in the attack, but he came from Zavidovici when the road was opened to Vozuca. And I had this meeting with him. We were standing next to a check-point formed by the Mujahedin Detachment. They formed it to prevent the participants in the attack to take war booty and especially weapons, except, of course, their own people. At that check-point there were two commanders of the Mujahedin Detachment, the Egyptian El Mu'utaz El Misri, who carried out the attack on -- at Paljenik, and Enver Sha'aban also. While we were talking, these two Mujahedin leaders and myself and Sead Brkic [phoen], I remember seeing two trucks going towards that check-point, and they stopped there for inspection. I didn't know where the trucks were coming from, but later I learnt that they were coming from Ozren, because most of the members of the Mujahedin Detachment were already at Mount Ozren. I noticed that one of those two trucks had blood dripping out of it, and Sead Brkic saw this, Enver Sha'aban, and El Mu'utaz. I was curious to see what was in those two trucks, as they were covered with canvas. In the first truck there was large quantity of weapons, mostly infantry weapons which the El Mujahedin Detachment had probably confiscated at Ozren. The second truck from which blood was dripping, I saw quite a number of bodies of killed soldiers. Some of them were wearing military uniforms, some were almost naked. And I saw that these killed men had no heads. I also noticed that among those corpses there were some heads, severed heads. I can't tell you how many, but roughly 20 or maybe a little less or a little more perhaps. I was watching Enver Sha'aban and El Mu'utaz El Misri, and I saw an expression of satisfaction on their faces. They were smiling and watching those bodies coldly, indifferently. Then I saw Sead Brkic's expression. I saw that he was angry. His expression had changed, and I thought to myself, Is Sead Brkic angry because of what we had seen in the bloody truck, or had he changed because the Mujahedin Detachment did not let his unit to take war booty, war bounty? Then Enver Sha'aban and El Mu'utaz started a discussion in raised voices and said, "You must remove this bloody truck straight away. Don't let the other soldiers see this." And after that, he continued talking to them, this Brkic, and he said why the Mujahedin did not allow his -- members of his unit to take part of the war booty, because they, too, had participated in the attack. And he said that without his unit the Mujahedin would not have liberated Paljenik, and had we not been at Gradic he would have done nothing at Paljenik. I'm telling you this whole story to show that Sead Urkic was aware of the fact that the Mujahedin had killed and slaughtered people. Now, whether he undertook anything or not, I don't know. Whether he took any steps or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... your long and detailed explanation. My last question is: If the Bosnian authorities, the ABiH commanders, had wanted to take any action against war crimes possibly committed by Mujahedin, would they, in your view, have been able to do so? Now, this is a question that you may not be able to answer, and if you don't -- can't answer it, then please tell me so, but if you know about discussions internally within the Mujahedin about possible reactions to an attempt by the ABiH commanders to discipline or perhaps prosecute crimes committed by the Mujahedin how the Mujahedin would have reacted to such an attempt. If you know about this, I would be pleased to know.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the I know -- or let me explain it differently. It's impossible that the B and H army, even though it wasn't formed properly, that it would -- was not able to prevent just a handful of Mujahedin no matter how many of them were there. If there were 100, 200, 300, even if there were a thousand of them, why would not the B and H army be able to prevent them? I know that we, the foreign Mujahedin, had something like immunity from the police. We enjoyed police immunity. We had somebody's support. Someone was backing us. I don't know who. I mentioned in my book several events which really do confirm that we were accepted here in Bosnia with all the bad things that we did -- or, rather, the Mujahedin did many bad things in public places. The police would come to them not to arrest them, but to ask them that they should not be doing this any more. For example, I would enter a coffee bar, cafe, where they are serving alcoholic drinks as well. I would just demolish everything. I'm not saying that I did this personally. I'm just using it as an example, because many Mujahedin did that during the war. So I still committed a criminal act. Somebody was supposed to prevent me. Whether from the BH army, whether it was the police, the military police, somebody of the local people from this country should have done something. All I know is that as long as I was the unit commander in Bijelo Bucje in 1993, they would come to me, policemen, military policemen. The policemen wore insignia OG from Travnik. And then they would say to me, "Please, your soldiers did this, this, and this. Can you please tell them that they are not allowed to do that, they shouldn't do that, it's not nice behaviour? People would hate us." So at the time my only conclusion was that even the police could not do its work in relation to the foreign Mujahedin if they were involved. I also know about one Mujahedin who was in my unit in 1993 or early 1994. He fired from a firearm at a vehicle which belonged to the international forces at the time. It was actually the British Battalion, the BritBat. And I know that earlier he wounded several of those soldiers, and he was arrested. He was arrested by the local police and spent about four months in detention. But after those four months he was released, no indictment was issued, and there was no prison sentence. So somebody worked to have him released. And after that the man disappeared. So that means that he was given the opportunity to evade responsibility on condition that he was no longer to stay in Bosnia. I can cite one more example. In 1994 in Zenica, a large number of Mujahedin lived in a village nine -- known by the name Olokov Polje [phoen]. The Mujahedin, many of them, about 20 men, were living there with their families in that village. I know about one of them, a Palestinian who was known as Ebu Besir. In the middle of the town, in the centre of Zenica, he stopped a vehicle with the plates or insignia of the IFOR at that time, and under threat that he would shoot at them, he got them out of the vehicle and confiscated the vehicle. It was a vehicle like a small personnel carrier. It was a military week. And he drove it in the centre of town, and nobody could do anything about it. The police saw it. So this was noted by the police. And nobody was arrested because of that. I know one thing, that he would always park that in front of husband house in Olokov Polje. I mean, if he had at least repainted the vehicle, changed the colour of the vehicle so that it wouldn't be obvious that it blocked to the international forces. However, he left it exactly the way it was. He was really sure and had the confidence that are nobody would do anything about it, or he knew that he was enjoying police immunity. I know that they sent about 50 policemen from Zenica to bring him in. I'm giving you this information that he told me himself, and I also heard it from other Mujahedin. You can imagine 50 police officers going to arrest one single person. When they reached his house, they knocked nicely as if they were guests. So it's not treatment of a person who was supposed to be arrested but they came as guests. He opened the door and he said, "What do you want from me?" They looked at him, they stretched -- they pointed to the vehicle, and they said that the soldiers of the international forces complained that he had seized their vehicle and that they demanded the authorities -- that the authorities arrest the person and that the vehicle be returned to them. So they asked him to go with them to the police station in Zenica. He responded impolitely, and he said, "Let me show you something." He went into the house and came out in a few seconds with a rifle in his hand, and they all hid wherever they were able to hide, behind anything, whether it was some kind of object or a car. In any case, what I want to say is that those 50 policemen returned to Zenica, and they were allegedly not able to arrest him. So there's the question of why. I believe that they were enjoying police immunity and that they had protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you, sir. Now when the Prosecutor asked you questions this afternoon, he started off by asking you if you ever became a member of the El Mujahid Detachment at any stage.
